text: This lesson walks one realistic mix of change types through everything Lessons 10 through 13 taught, end to end. Meridian Freight runs its ERP on a production database server and an application tier, and has three recurring kinds of change to classify, assess, and route correctly.

Monthly OS and application patching is the same action, on a known schedule, already reviewed once — a Standard change built from a Change Template. Finance and operations schema edits are different every time, so they're Normal changes. A rare middle-of-the-night ERP outage fix is an Emergency change, authorized fast by the on-call change manager plus one senior infrastructure lead, not full CAB.

For Normal changes, the risk assessment is built as a rules-based lookup rather than open-ended scoring, because one fact dominates: any change touching the production database is automatically forced to High risk, regardless of the other answers. The risk field stays read-only, calculated only from those real answers.

The two-stage approval flow chains manager approval first, then checks the calculated risk right after. A change to a non-production reporting sandbox resolves after manager approval alone. A change to the production database correctly picks up the second stage, CAB approval, because its risk comes back High.

When operations schedules an index change on the production database for Saturday night, Conflict Detection automatically flags it against an already-scheduled firmware update on the same server with an overlapping window — before the CAB even meets. Supported by the Change Calendar's view of that weekend, the board resolves it by rescheduling the index change rather than letting both run concurrently.

Classification, risk calculation, chained approval, and conflict detection all connecting automatically is what separates defining the three change types from actually implementing Change Enablement. Next up: Chapter Four begins with the Request and Requested Item tables.
